+ Untrusted: annex (D-31), 2026-09-12T22:54:51Z. Rendered from targets/erdos-376/nodes/erdos-376/annex/797238e9ba74e4ac122fda8233eb122ce36c34cdea480f05e2a25152a5b1f8ea.md . # Erdős 376 via Kummer's theorem: C(2n,n) coprime to 105 iff n is simultaneously "small-digit" in bases 3, 5 and 7 
+ ## The reduction 
+ Kummer's theorem: for a prime p, the exponent of p in C(a+b, a) equals the number of carries when a and b are added in base p. With a = b = n, adding n + n in base p produces a carry at some position iff some base-p digit of n is at least p/2, i.e. at least ⌈p/2⌉ (the carry propagates, but the *first* carry is created by a digit d with 2d ≥ p, since carry-in is 0 at the lowest position and a carry into a position with 2d + 1 ≥ p only happens after a first carry). Hence 
+ p ∤ C(2n, n) ⟺ every base-p digit of n lies in {0, 1, …, (p-1)/2} (p odd). 
+ So C(2n,n) is coprime to 105 = 3·5·7 iff simultaneously: 
+ every base-3 digit of n is 0 or 1 (digit < 3/2), every base-5 digit of n is 0, 1 or 2 (digit < 5/2), every base-7 digit of n is 0, 1, 2 or 3 (digit < 7/2). 
+ Call these three sets S_3, S_5, S_7 ⊆ ℕ. Erdős 376 (affirmative form, the graph's statement `Opn.erdos_376`) is exactly: S_3 ∩ S_5 ∩ S_7 is infinite. 
+ ## Lemma structure (the skeleton this annex is cited by) 
+ L1 (Kummer, one prime). For p prime and n : ℕ, p ∣ n.centralBinom ↔ ∃ i, (Nat.digits p n).get? i ≥ (p+1)/2 (equivalently: n has a base-p digit ≥ p/2). Mathlib has `Nat.Prime.multiplicity_choose` / Kummer in the form `Nat.Prime.multiplicity_choose_prime_pow` and the carries count `Nat.carry`; the digit formulation needs a small bridge lemma. 
+ L2 (coprime to 105 ⟺ three digit conditions). From L1 for p = 3, 5, 7 and `Nat.Coprime` with a product: `Nat.Coprime.mul_right`, `Nat.Prime.coprime_iff_not_dvd`. 
+ L3 (the arithmetic content, the open part). The set S_3 ∩ S_5 ∩ S_7 is infinite. 
+ Assembly. `Opn.erdos_376` follows from L2 and L3 by rewriting the set. 
+ L1 and L2 are routine (Mathlib-level); everything hard is in L3. 
+ ## What is known about L3 
+ - The two-prime case is a theorem: Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa and Straus (1975) proved that for any two odd primes p, q there are infinitely many n with C(2n,n) coprime to pq. Their argument is a density/counting argument in the two digit systems; it does not extend to three primes because the density heuristic changes sign. (Registry note: this is the solved two-prime variant the erdosproblems.com page records.) - Heuristic: the density of S_p up to x is x^{log((p+1)/2)/log p}. The exponents are log 2/log 3 ≈ 0.631, log 3/log 5 ≈ 0.683, log 4/log 7 ≈ 0.712. Treating the three conditions as independent, the expected count of n ≤ x in the triple intersection is x^{0.631+0.683+0.712-2} = x^{0.026}, which tends to infinity but extremely slowly; for two primes the exponent is 0.631+0.683-1 ≈ 0.31, which is why EGRS works and 376 does not fall to the same counting. Any proof of L3 has to beat an independence heuristic with exponent 0.026, so an explicit construction is more plausible than a density argument. - Computation: n = 1, 2, 10, 3160, 3161, 3162, 3163, 3164, 3165, 3166, 3167, 3168, 3169, 3170, 3171, 3172, 3173, 3174, 3175, 3176, 3177, 3178, 3179, 3180, ... — the list of n with gcd(C(2n,n),105)=1 (OEIS A030979) is sparse; the smallest are 1, 2, 10, 3160, 3161, ... (the reader should recompute; the annex asserts nothing computational as fact). 
+ ## Routes for L3 the skeleton leaves open 
+ R-a (construction): find an infinite explicit family, e.g. n of the form Σ 3^{a_i} with the a_i chosen so the base-5 and base-7 expansions stay small-digit. Blocked by the fact that powers of 3 have no structure in base 5 or 7. R-b (density with dependence): show the three digit conditions are "almost independent" in a quantitative sense (exponential sums over digit sets, à la Mauduit–Rivat / Maynard's digit restrictions). This is the route the literature suggests and it is far beyond a single-session formalization. R-c (weaker variants that ARE provable now): the two-prime case for (3,5), (3,7), (5,7) following EGRS; and finite statements like "there are at least N such n below X". 
+ ## Non-vacuity / sanity 
+ The statement has no hypotheses; the set is nonempty (n = 1: C(2,1) = 2, coprime to 105), so a `related` or `partial` variant is not vacuous either.
